text:
The hall at the Calder Vane Foundation was still settling into its seats on 14 March when Tobias Wrenfield, chair of the jury, stepped to the lectern with the citation in hand. He read slowly, as though the pause before the name were part of the tradition.

It was Mireille Ashgrove who stood to applause, this year's winner of the Calder Vane Prize for architecture.

The prize has long been regarded as a measure of where the profession is heading, and this year's field was broad: 212 projects were submitted. The award carries 85,000 vane-marks.

In its published "Statement of the Calder Vane Architecture Jury," the panel singled out Ashgrove's Lowmere Harbour Pavilion for praise. Wrenfield, reading from that text, offered no flourish. The building, it seemed, was meant to speak for itself.
